			<div class="ArticlePage-lede">
				<div class="ArticlePage-lede-content">
					<h1 class="Page-headline">
						US soybean oil demand moves up again in September as soybean oil stocks slide to 12-year low					</h1>
											<h2 class="Page-subHeadline">
							For a seventh consecutive month, implied US soybean oil consumption moved up in September, as stockpiles declined to their lowest level since 2014.						</h2>
									</div>
			</div>
			<div class="ArticlePage-info-wrapper">
				<div class="ArticlePage-info">
					<div class="Page-byline">
						<div class="Page-datePublished">
							October 19, 2026						</div>
													<div class="Page-authors">
								<span>By</span>
								<a href="https://www.fastmarkets.com/about-us/people/amanda-luhavalja/" aria-label="Amanda Luhavalja">Amanda Luhavalja</a>							</div>
											</div>
											<div class="Page-tags">
															<a class="Link" href="https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/category/agriculture/"
									aria-label="Agriculture"
									data-style="" data-cms-ai="0">
									Agriculture								</a>
															<a class="Link" href="https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/category/commodity/soy/"
									aria-label="Soy"
									data-style="" data-cms-ai="0">
									Soy								</a>
															<a class="Link" href="https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/category/commodity/soy-oil/"
									aria-label="Soy oil"
									data-style="" data-cms-ai="0">
									Soy oil								</a>
													</div>
									</div>
			</div>
			<div class="Page-articleBody">
				<div class="RichTextArticleBody RichTextBody">
					
<p>Data released by the National Oilseed Processors Association (NOPA) on October 15 showed that <a href="https://www.fastmarkets.com/agriculture/veg-oils-and-meals/soybean-oil-prices/">soybean oil stocks</a> among members were down by 12.3% on the month to 1.05 billion pounds in September, from 1.20 billion pounds in August.</p>



<p>The latest stock figure was also down by 15.3% from 1.24 billion pounds of soybean oil in September 2025. NOPA members process about 99% of all US soybeans.</p>



<p>In the US, soybean oil is the primary vegetable oil feedstock used in the production of biomass-based diesel and renewable diesel fuel. Demand for soybean oil started to increase earlier in the year, particularly from the biofuel sector, amid increased clarity regarding the 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit and the finalization of 2026-2027 Renewable Volume Obligations (RVOs) biofuel blending mandates.</p>



<p>Still, in the last month or so, biofuel sector demand for soybean oil and other feedstocks slowed, market sources said, with several biofuel production plants reportedly offline for planned and unplanned maintenance at the US Gulf Coast and in the Midwest.</p>



<p>The latest NOPA data also showed that as US soybean oil stocks continued to decrease, soybean crush also extended lower in September, slipping to a 13-month low at 196.3 million bushels. The September crush was down by 4.4% from 205.456 million bushels in August.</p>



<p>Trading sources attributed the sharp month-on-month decline in soybean crush to a normal seasonal slowdown in operations and a weather-related slowdown in processing across the western US Corn Belt. In the second half of September, crushers struggled to procure soybeans following heavy rains in parts of the Midwest that impacted soybean quality and caused harvest delays. Crushers in and around Iowa were the most impacted, with some running tight or out of soybeans, trading sources said.</p>



<p>US soybean crush hit record highs earlier this year amid solid processing margins and strong domestic soybean oil demand. The crush industry has been expanding since 2021, with the build-out progressing through facility upgrades and the construction of new plants to meet increased demand for soybean oil from the US biofuel and food and feed sectors.</p>



<p>In mid-September, CHS announced it would proceed with the construction of a proposed $770 million processing plant near Evansville, Wisconsin. The new facility will have the capacity to process 80 million bushels of soybeans each year. Completion is targeted for the fall of 2028.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-full"><img fetchpriority="high" width="627" height="541" decoding="async" src="https://www.fastmarkets.com/tachyon/2026/10/Soybean-oil-2.png" alt="" class="wp-image-138347" srcset="https://www.fastmarkets.com/tachyon/2026/10/Soybean-oil-2.png?resize=627%2C541&zoom=1 627w, https://www.fastmarkets.com/tachyon/2026/10/Soybean-oil-2.png?resize=627%2C541&zoom=0.5 314w, https://www.fastmarkets.com/tachyon/2026/10/Soybean-oil-2.png?resize=627%2C541&zoom=0.25 157w" sizes="(max-width: 627px) 100vw, 627px" /></figure>



<p>In its monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) released Friday October 9, USDA maintained its outlook for 2026-2027 US soybean oil consumption for biofuel production at 17.8 billion pounds. This is up by 22% from an expected 14.55 billion pounds in the 2025-2026 season. US soybean oil demand from all industry sectors was anticipated to reach 30.305 billion pounds in 2025-2026 and roughly 33.11 billion pounds in the 2026-2027 season.</p>



<p>USDA remains bullish on US soybean oil consumption heading into 2027 following the finalization of RVOs earlier this spring that expanded feedstock demand from the biofuel sector. Under the US Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), obligated parties, which include oil refiners, must blend billions of gallons of biofuel into the US fuel mix or purchase Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) from other blenders or producers each year.</p>



<p>The latest EMTS data showed the biomass-based diesel industry is ramping up production to meet the stronger renewable blending volumes established under Set 2. D4 RIN generation reached 753 million in September, up by 8.7% from August and by 13.7% from September 2025. </p>

Soybean oil prices fall amid new US biofuel proposals

11:50, 15 October 2026
Source:  Spglobal

Soybean oil futures on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) extended their decline on October 14 amid uncertainty over US biofuel policy and increasing supplies of newly harvested soybeans. The December contract fell by 1.34% to 67.11 cents/lb during the first half of the trading session, down 4.24% from the previous session’s intraday high. On October 13, prices had climbed to 70.08 cents/lb before closing at 68.02 cents/lb, down 0.89%.

The main factor weighing on the market was a new proposal announced by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on October 13. The agency proposed reallocating approximately 770 mln Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) associated with exemptions granted to small refineries from renewable fuel obligations. The total volume of exemptions for 2025 amounted to 1.76 billion RINs, compared with the previously anticipated 990 mln. The reallocation is intended to preserve renewable fuel requirements, supporting demand for feedstocks used in biofuel production, particularly soybean oil.

The EPA is considering two options for implementing the proposal: distributing the additional obligations equally between 2026 and 2027 or assigning the entire volume to 2027. No final decision has been made, and the public comment period will remain open until December 4. According to market participants, full reallocation had already been largely priced in, limiting the proposal’s ability to provide sustained support for futures. Instead, uncertainty over the implementation timeline increased volatility in soybean oil prices.

Additional pressure on the market is coming from the accelerating US soybean harvest. According to USDA, as of October 11, American farmers had harvested 46% of soybean acreage, compared with 25% a week earlier. However, harvesting progress remains below the five-year average of 50%. Increasing arrivals of newly harvested soybeans are accompanied by more active commercial hedging, adding downward pressure on oilseed futures.

The recent price decline highlights the US soybean oil market’s sensitivity to government regulation of the biofuel sector. On October 7, December CBOT soybean oil futures had already fallen by 3.19% in a single trading session, settling at 67.68 cents/lb. Future price movements will largely depend on the EPA’s final decisions regarding the allocation of biofuel obligations between 2026 and 2027, as well as the pace of new soybean crop deliveries and demand from the processing industry.

        <p class="remove-margin back-to-text"><strong><a href="https://soygrowers.com/news-releases/" class="txt-brand-color-1"><i class="far fa-long-arrow-alt-left txt-brand-color-1 add-padding-right mod-padding-half back-to-icon "></i>Back</a></strong></p>

            <div class="blog-post add-margin-bottom">
                <h2 class="add-margin-bottom">Has Biofuel Demand Replaced Export Demand in U.S. Soybean Markets?</h2>
                <p class="date txt-brand-color-4">Oct 14, 2026</p>
                                <div class="copy add-padding-top mod-padding-x2">
                    <p><em>By ASA Economics Intern Taylor Gillit & ASA Chief Economist Scott Gerlt, PhD</em></p>
<p>For decades, export demand was the primary driver of growth for the U.S. soybean industry. Recently, challenges in export markets have coincided with the rapid expansion of domestic demand for soybean oil used as a biofuel feedstock in renewable diesel and biodiesel.</p>
<p>Between 2020 and 2025, the quantity of soybean oil allocated to biofuel production increased from nearly 8.9 billion pounds to approximately 14 billion pounds, creating an important new source of domestic demand and encouraging investment in soybean crushing capacity (Figure 1). At the same time, export demand remains below historical levels, raising an important economic question: <strong>Has growing domestic biofuel demand been sufficient to offset weaker export demand to maintain U.S. soybean prices?</strong></p>
<h4><em>Figure 1</em></h4>
<p><img class="aligncenter wp-image-38202 " src="https://soygrowers.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/fig-1.png" alt="" width="807" height="455" /></p>
<h3 style="text-align: left;"><strong><em>Methods</em></strong></h3>
<p>To answer this question, an updated eeconomic model<a href="#_ftn1" name="_ftnref1">[1] </a>of the U.S. soybean sector was used to estimate soybean price impacts from current events including trade shocks and increases in biofuel blending obligations. Counterfactual scenarios of export demand and soybean oil demand for biofuel production remaining at marketing year (MY) 23/24 levels were observed for this analysis. Comparing these benchmark market conditions with subsequent market conditions allows a measurement of weaker whole bean export demand and stronger domestic biofuel demand on soy prices (whole bean, oil, and meal), as well as commodity revenues.</p>
<p>Importantly, demand curves were set to the MY 23/24 levels for the selected variables. Supply and demand curves for all other variables were unchanged from their current years. A demand curve measures changes in quantity demanded due to a change in price. It is not the actual quantity but a mapping of prices to quantities. An easy way to interpret these results is to view the price change as the loss or gain experienced from the change in the exports from MY 23/24 levels. All the results should be compared to the MY 23/24 demand and should not be regarded as the total value of the sector.</p>
<p>This analysis allows for an examination of price impacts both without the changes in whole soybean export demand and domestic biofuel demand since MY 23/24. The model does not consider specific events, such as foreign tariffs or changes in blending obligations. Instead, it captures all developments in the market. As such, it also reflects crop conditions in South America, changes in biofuel tax policy, competing biofuel feedstock imports and other developments.</p>
<p>The MY 24/25 to MY 26/27 market years were considered in the analysis. Additionally, soybean production was held constant for MY 25/26 to analyze price responses when export demand changes after the growing season had already begun. The trade war with China started in February 2025 and escalated in April 2025, limiting farmers’ ability to respond through acreage adjustments. The MY 25/26 and MY 26/27 marketing years have not been finalized, so the October 2026 USDA World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) estimates and revisions were used as the baseline for those years.</p>
<h3><strong><em>Changes in Whole Soybean Prices</em></strong></h3>
<p>Export demand remains an important driver of soybean prices across the observed period, although the relative influence of trade and biofuel demand varies by marketing year. In MY 24/25 and MY 25/26, changes in export demand consistently have a larger effect on soybean prices. Conversely, in MY 26/27, the estimated positive effect of biofuel demand offsets the negative effect of changes in export demand. Table 1 reports the estimated contribution of changes in export demand and soybean oil demand for biofuel production to soybean prices.</p>
<h4><em>Table 1. Estimated Change in Soybean Price from 2023/24 Demand Levels ($/bushel)</em></h4>
<p><img class="aligncenter wp-image-38212 size-large" src="https://soygrowers.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Table-1-2-1024x181.png" alt="" width="1024" height="181" />Changes in export demand since MY 23/24 accounted for an estimated $0.81 per bushel decline in soybean prices in MY 24/25. Changes in domestic biofuel demand contributed an additional $0.06 per bushel decline, resulting in a combined estimated price reduction of $0.87 per bushel. The biofuel effect on soybeans was $0.06 per bushel lower in MY 24/25 than in MY 23/24. This was due to low 2023-2025 renewable volume obligations through the Renewable Fuel Standard, which triggered volume reductions at many biodiesel facilities in early 2025. The biofuel tax credit changed from $1.00 per gallon in 2024 (40A Biofuel Blenders Credit) to a lower and variable rate in 2025 (45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit). Soybean oil volumes used in biofuels plummeted in early 2025. Production accelerated in 2024 to maximize the credit value, leading to a collapse in 2025 Biomass-Based Diesel (BBD) production after low blending obligations could not support the production.</p>
<p>More recent years tell a somewhat different story. Relative to MY 23/24 demand conditions, weaker export demand continues to account for the largest decline in soybean prices, reducing prices by as much as $1.60 per bushel under the projected MY 25/26 market conditions. Holding soybean production fixed for MY 25/26 illustrates how prices respond when producers cannot adjust production following the sudden decline in export demand. Under this assumption, the estimated price decline increases to $2.10 per bushel because more of the market adjustment occurs through prices rather than production.</p>
<p>This sharp decline occurred during the period of trade disruptions with China. While the country historically buys 22 MMT or more of U.S. soy per marketing year, China is on track to purchase a little over 12 MMT in marketing year MY 26/27. However, export demand has weakened every year since MY 23/24. Part of the decline in prices is due Brazil producing a short crop in MY 23/24 while China’s import demand remained high. Since then, Brazilian production has increased every year since the MY 23/24 drought, shifting the excess demand curve for U.S. soy inward.</p>
<p>The resumption of normal soybean exports to China is expected to have a marked effect on soy prices for MY 26/27. The year-over-year increase is estimated at about $1.40 to $1.90 per bushel, depending on assumptions about how much MY 25/26 production responded to the trade war. This result is based on October 2026 WASDE projections which are subject to change as the marketing year develops. As such, the MY 26/27 results should be treated as provisional.</p>
<p>In contrast, projected growth in domestic biofuel demand provides upward support for soybean prices, increasing prices above MY 23/24 levels by an estimated $0.22 per bushel in MY 25/26 and $0.42 per bushel in MY 26/27. Expanding biofuel production drives a recovery in soybean oil use for biofuels and adds value to soybeans. The MY 25/26 marketing year reflects a $0.22-per-bushel increase in value due to biofuel demand, with another $0.20 per bushel expected for the crop currently in the ground. The value-add from biofuels is projected to support capacity growth in the biofuel and crush industries for at least the next three years.</p>
<p>Although increasing biofuel demand has lifted soybean prices, the gains have been less than the fall from export demand through MY 25/26. In MY 24/25, the net of the two was a decrease of $0.87 per bushel. For MY 25/26, the estimate is $1.38 to $1.81 loss per bushel, depending on assumptions about farmers' ability to respond to the market conditions. The $0.22 to $0.29 per bushel in market gain from biofuels simply was not enough to offset the trade losses of $1.60 to $2.10 per bushel. However, revived soybean export purchases from China and the expanding value of biofuels are projected to have a net price increase of $0.18 per bushel in MY 26/27, conditional on the October 2026 WASDE estimates and projections being realized.</p>
<h3><em><strong>Changes in Soybean Oil Prices</strong> </em></h3>
<p>Soybean oil is directly used as a feedstock for biomass-based diesel and renewable diesel production, making domestic biofuel demand a key driver of soybean oil prices. While weaker whole soybean export demand reduces soybean oil prices by increasing domestic supply of whole soybeans, projected growth in biofuel demand more than offsets the export effect under the projected market conditions. Table 2 reports the estimated contribution of changes in whole soybean export demand and soybean oil demand for biofuel production to soybean oil prices.</p>
<h4><em>Table 2. Estimated Change in Soybean Oil Price (¢/pound)</em></h4>
<p><img class="aligncenter wp-image-38209 size-large" src="https://soygrowers.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/TABLE-2-1-1024x179.png" alt="" width="1024" height="179" /></p>
<p>Weaker export whole soybean demand reduced soybean oil prices by an estimated 1.80 cents per pound under observed MY 24/25 market conditions. At the same time, lower domestic biofuel demand reduced soybean oil prices by an additional 2.17 cents per pound over the marketing year, reflecting reduced soybean oil demand for biofuel production from MY 23/24 levels following the reduced output of biomass-based diesel during 2025. Because export demand and biofuel demand were both weaker than in the MY 23/24 benchmark year, their effects reinforced one another, resulting in soybean oil prices 3.97 cents per pound lower than under MY 23/24 demand conditions.</p>
<p>The projected market conditions for MY 25/26 and MY 26/27 tell a different story. While weaker export demand places downward pressure on soybean oil prices, projected growth in domestic biofuel demand becomes the dominant force affecting the soybean oil market. Because soybean oil is the primary feedstock for biodiesel and renewable diesel production, expanding biofuel production directly increases demand for soybean oil, raising its value.</p>
<p>The projected increase in soybean oil demand reflects biodiesel and renewable diesel production recovery from the temporary slowdown observed in 2025. As a result, the positive contribution of biofuel demand grows from 8.39 cents per pound in MY 25/26 to 15.67 cents per pound in MY 26/27, more than offsetting the downward pressure associated with weaker export demand. Holding soybean production fixed in MY 25/26 produces slightly larger price effects, reinforcing how limited short-run production adjustments amplify the market's response to changes in demand.</p>
<p>Consequently, the combined effect reduces soybean oil prices by 3.97 cents per pound in MY 24/25 that reverse to gains in MY 25/26 and MY 26/27, relative to MY 23/24 demand conditions. These results illustrate how soybean oil prices have become increasingly influenced by domestic energy markets as well as traditional agricultural markets. While export demand continues to affect soybean oil prices indirectly through changes in soybean crushing, expanding biofuel production increasingly determines the value of soybean oil itself.</p>
<h3><em><strong>Changes in Soybean Meal Prices</strong> </em></h3>
<p>Soybean meal is a coproduct of soybean crushing, therefore its price depends on not just soybean meal demand, but also soybean oil demand. More soybeans are crushed for soybean oil when domestic biofuel demand increases which raises soybean meal production and places downward pressure on soybean meal prices. Combined with weaker export whole soybean demand, these markets result in substantially lower soybean meal prices than if export demand and domestic biofuel demand had remained at MY 23/24 levels.</p>
<h4><em>Table 3. Estimated Change in Soybean Meal Price ($/short ton) </em></h4>
<p><span style="letter-spacing: 0px;"><img class="aligncenter wp-image-38210 size-large" src="https://soygrowers.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/TABLE-3-1-1024x184.png" alt="" width="1024" height="184" />Under observed MY 24/25 market conditions, soybean meal prices were also influenced by changes in both export and domestic biofuel demand relative to MY 23/24. Weaker export demand lowered soybean meal prices by an estimated $11.61 per short ton. However, because domestic biofuel demand remained below MY 23/24 levels, its effect moved in the opposite direction. Soybean meal prices increased by approximately $3.78 per short ton from biofuels, partially offsetting the export-related decline.</span></p>
<p>Like soybean oil, under the projected market conditions both demand factors contribute to lower soybean meal prices, although for different reasons. The effect of weaker whole soybean export demand remains negative throughout the projection period, while stronger domestic biofuel demand increasingly lowers soybean meal prices by expanding soybean processing and, consequently, soybean meal production. By MY 26/27, the estimated price effect from stronger biofuel demand reaches a $27.24-per-short-ton reduction, compared with the $3.44-per-short-ton effect associated with weaker export demand. These results suggest growth in domestic biofuel demand becomes the primary source of downward pressure on soybean meal prices.</p>
<h3><em><strong>Commodity Revenue</strong> </em></h3>
<p>Commodity revenues reflect the combined effects of changes in prices and production and therefore provide a broad measure of how changes in export and domestic biofuel demand affect the soybean sector. Table 4 reports the estimated contribution of each demand source to soybean commodity revenues relative to MY 23/24 demand conditions.</p>
<h4><em>Table 4. Estimated Change in Commodity Revenue Effects (billions) </em></h4>
<p><img class="aligncenter wp-image-38211 size-large" src="https://soygrowers.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/TABLE-4-1-1024x289.png" alt="" width="1024" height="289" />Relative to MY 23/24 demand for soybean exports, MY 24/25 soy producers lost at least $3.55 billion due to reduced demand from foreign markets. Although lower domestic biofuel demand also contributed to lower revenues, its effect was considerably smaller. Looking ahead, projected growth in domestic biofuel demand provides increased support for soybean commodity revenues. However, under the projected MY 26/27 market conditions, the contribution of stronger biofuel demand does replace the revenue losses associated with weaker export demand, conditional on the October 2026 WASDE projections.</p>
<p>These results illustrate how the U.S. soybean market has evolved in recent years. Expanding domestic biofuel production has created an important new source of demand for soybean oil, encouraging investment in crushing capacity and increasing domestic soybean utilization. This growth has also expanded soybean meal supplies and strengthened the links between biofuel, livestock feed, and food markets due to the soy crush process dynamics. The benefits of growing biofuel demand therefore extend beyond soybean oil alone, influencing markets throughout the soybean value chain.</p>
<p>At the same time, the results suggest expanding domestic biofuel demand has supplemented export demand, and under projected MY 26/27 market conditions, replaces the losses associated with weaker export demand. However, this finding is conditional on the October 2026 WASDE projections being realized, and changes in projected export or biofuel demand could alter the relative contributions of these markets. As U.S. soybean exports face increasing competition from Brazil and periods of trade uncertainty, continued growth in domestic biofuel production provides an important source of market stability and diversifies demand across domestic markets. Maintaining competitive export markets remains essential, as export demand continues to play a significant role in soybean prices and commodity revenues, even as domestic biofuel demand takes a larger role.</p>

The U.S. average soybean yield forecast stands at 53.1 bushels per acre, up 0.3 bushels per acre from last month’s projection. With higher soybean production and lower beginning stocks, total soybean supply is raised by 17 million bushels to 4.9 billion bushels. Soybean exports are raised by 10 million bushels to nearly 1.7 billion bushels on higher supplies. Soybean crush is unchanged this month and stands at 2.78 billion bushels. The soybean ending stocks for MY 2026/27 are forecast at 315 million bushels, marginally higher than last month’s forecast and even with last year’s finalized ending stocks. The soybean price received by farmers forecast for 2026/27 is unchanged at $12.00 per bushel. The USDA, National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) published the first production forecast for U.S. canola and sunflowerseed in this month’s Crop Production report. U.S. canola production is forecast at a record of 5.4 billion pounds on record acreage. U.S. sunflowerseed production is forecast at 2.3 billion pounds, 31 million pounds lower than MY 2025/26 sunflowerseed production. Indonesia’s palm oil production is lowered this month by 2.2 million metric tons to 45 million metric tons on reduced yields. Yield is forecast at 3.21 metric tons per hectare, nearly 5 percent lower than last month’s forecast due to dryness in the major palm oil producing provinces of Sumatra and Kalimantan. Economic Research Service | Situation and Outlook Report Next release is November 13, 2026 OCS-26j | October 14, 2026 In this report: - Domestic Outlook - International Outlook -- 1 of 10 -- 2 Oil Crops Outlook: October 2026, OCS-26j, October 14, 2026 USDA, Economic Research Service Domestic Outlook Soybean Outlook In its Crop Production report this month, USDA, National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) forecasts the MY 2026/27 U.S. soybean production at 4.56 billion bushels, up 27 million bushels from last month’s forecast. The U.S. average soybean yield forecast is up 0.3 bushels per acre and stands at 53.1 bushels per acre. The harvested acreage is unchanged this month at 85.9 million acres. Higher soybean yield estimates contributed to the increase in aggregate U.S. soybean production. Yield estimates were higher month to month for Arkansas, Illinois, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, North Dakota, Ohio, South Carolina, and Tennessee. Higher month-to-month harvests in these States more than offset lower estimated production in: Alabama, Kansas, Iowa, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, and Wisconsin. Overall, while there is higher soybean production across the corn belt and the delta regions, the Northern and Central Plains regions are projected to have smaller soybean crops than last year. September 2026 was dominated by persistent heavy rainfall across the Western Corn Belt and Central Plains regions (especially Nebraska, Kansas, and Iowa)—leading to repeated harvest delays, localized flooding, and record-breaking monthly precipitation. While these rains improved soil moisture after earlier dryness, the rains also created field access issues during early harvest, with these States seeing less than 3 days suitable for fieldwork. Iowa was only at 5 percent harvested compared to a 5 year average of 38 percent, Kansas at 16 percent harvested versus 22 percent, and Nebraska at 9 percent harvested versus 34 percent. As a result, the U.S soybean harvest was only 25 percent complete as of October 4, compared to 5- year average of 33 percent. In addition, there have been reports of lower quality soybeans due to these heavy rains. The beginning stocks for MY 2026/27 were lower than previously estimated. USDA, NASS indicated in its latest Grain Stocks report that the September 1 soybean inventory totaled 315.1 million bushels. Off-farm stocks were reported at 224.7 million bushels and accounted for 71 percent of total soybean stocks. The lower carry-in stocks from MY 2025/26 are more than offset by higher soybean production, raising the total soybean supply forecast for the MY 2026/27 by 17 million bushels to 4.9 billion bushels. With higher soybean supply, the U.S. soybean export forecast is raised by 10 million bushels to 1.7 billion bushels. The soybean -- 2 of 10 -- 3 Oil Crops Outlook: October 2026, OCS-26j, October 14, 2026 USDA, Economic Research Service crush forecast is unchanged this month and stands at 2.78 billion bushels. Noticeably, there are small changes to the soybean balance sheet for MY 2025/26, as the crush and trade data are finalized for the September–August marketing year. U.S. soybean crush for MY 2025/26 is finalized at 2,646 million bushels, 9 million bushels lower than last month’s forecast due to lower-than-expected crush in August. August soybean crush was reported at 209.6 million bushels, which was lower than expected due to additional seasonal downtime. U.S. soybean ending stocks for MY 2026/27 are forecast at 315 million bushels, up from last month’s forecast and unchanged year to year from the revised MY 2025/26 ending stocks estimate. The MY 2026/27 season-average farm soybean price forecast is unchanged this month and stands at $12 per bushel. In September, soybean prices in Central Illinois at the elevators rallied on slow harvest progress and tighter soybean stocks and reached a monthly average of $12.96 per bushel, compared to $12.08 in August and at $9.84 same time last year (figure 1). Despite this rally, the season-average soybean farm price forecast remains unchanged from last month, as prices are expected to be under pressure once harvest supplies start to hit the market in late October. 6.00 8.00 10.00 12.00 14.00 16.00 18.00 Sep-21 Nov-21 Jan-22 Mar-22 May-22 Jul-22 Sep-22 Nov-22 Jan-23 Mar-23 May-23 Jul-23 Sep-23 Nov-23 Jan-24 Mar-24 May-24 Jul-24 Sep-24 Nov-24 Jan-25 Mar-25 May-25 Jul-25 Sep-25 Nov-25 Jan-26 Mar-26 May-26 Jul-26 Sep-26 Dollars per bushel Figure 1 U.S. central Illinois county elevator soybean price Source: USDA, Economic Research Service using data from USDA, Agricultural Marketing Service, Illinois Grain Bids report. -- 3 of 10 -- 4 Oil Crops Outlook: October 2026, OCS-26j, October 14, 2026 USDA, Economic Research Service U.S. Soybean Meal and Oil Imports Are Raised for MY 2026/27 The U.S. soybean meal supply for MY 2026/27 is increased this month on higher soybean meal imports. Soybean meal imports are raised to 1.0 million short tons, slightly below revised imports for MY 2025/26. U.S. soybean meal imports for MY 2025/26 are raised this month due to higher-than-expected imports in August. In the October–August period of MY 2025/26, the United States imported most of its soybean meal from Canada, Togo, Nigeria, Argentina, and Turkey (figure 2). Organic soybean meal imports account for more than 60 percent of the total soybean meal imports in MY 2025/26 and are mostly supplied by following countries: Togo, Nigeria, Turkey, Canada, and Benin. Higher soybean meal imports are expected to be consumed domestically. Consequently, domestic soybean meal consumption is raised to 44.1 million short tons, reflecting a nearly 2- percent growth in domestic consumption. The soybean meal average price for MY 2026/27 is forecast at $340.00 per short ton, unchanged from last month’s forecast. In contrast, the soybean oil supply forecast for MY 2026/27 (October-September) is reduced by 80 million pounds this month to 35.3 billion pounds on lower beginning stocks from MY 2025/26, partially offset by higher soybean oil imports. Soybean oil stocks for the year ending September 2026 have tightened on lower soybean oil production in MY 2025/26. Soybean oil production in MY 2025/26 (October-September) is lowered on a decrease in soybean crush for the last 2 months of the October–September marketing year and a reduced soybean oil extraction rate. Consequently, soybean oil ending stocks for MY 2025/26 are forecast at 1.66 billion pounds, 180 million pounds lower than last month’s forecast. U.S. soybean oil imports for MY 2026/27 are raised to 0.7 billion pounds, up 0.175 billion pounds from revised imports for MY 2025/26. Demand for soybean oil has stayed robust, particularly for use in biofuel production. The U.S. Department of Energy’s U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Feedstocks Consumed for Production of Biofuels report (dated September 30) showed 1.687 billion pounds of soybean oil were used in biofuels during July 2026, a new monthly record high. This number was 8.4 percent higher than the previous record observed in June 2026. The forecasts for soybean oil use in biofuel production for MY 2025/26 and MY 2026/27 are unchanged this month at 14.8 billion pounds and 17.8 billion pounds, respectively. The MY 2026/27 average price for soybean oil is unchanged at 70 cents per pound. Canola Production Reaches a Record on Acreage Expansion In the USDA, NASS October Crop Production report, NASS released updated canola acreage statistics. The report utilizes data from the USDA, Farm Service Agency and USDA, Risk Management Agency, along with its first survey-based yield forecast. In MY 2026/27, canola production is forecast at 5.4 billion pounds on additional canola acreage while yield is forecast to decline from last year. North Dakota (the leading canola producer) planted 2.33 million acres, up 29 percent from last year. The strong demand for vegetable oils both for food and use in biofuels supported canola prices, resulting in favorable returns compared to other commodities. Canola acreage also expanded in Minnesota, Montana, Washington, Oklahoma, and Kansas. Based on conditions during the growing season, canola yields are forecast to be down 10 percent from last year to 1,811 pounds per acre. -- 5 of 10 -- 6 Oil Crops Outlook: October 2026, OCS-26j, October 14, 2026 USDA, Economic Research Service With higher canola supply compared to MY 2025/26, U.S. canola usage is forecast to be up 16 percent from MY 2025/26. U.S. canola exports for MY 2026/27 are forecast to rise to 0.9 billion pounds, up from last month and last year. Total U.S. canola exports in the first quarter totaled 285 million pounds, up 170 million from last year. This increase is largely driven by additional shipments to Mexico and the Netherlands. Domestic canola crush is also forecast to be up 11 percent from MY 2025/26 to 5.3 billion pounds. In August 2026, NASS reported that 459.6 million pounds of canola were crushed. This number brought the first quarter crush total to 1.3 billion pounds, 15 percent higher than the first quarter in MY 2025/26. In addition, a new crush facility is expected to be completed in MY 2026/27, expanding the total U.S. canola crush capacity. This expansion of crush is largely supported by the domestic demand for canola oil and canola meal, which has supported domestic crush margins. The additional production of canola oil and meal is forecast to be used largely domestically. In MY 2026/27, biofuel use of canola oil is forecast to expand to 5.6 billion pounds, up from 3.7 billion pounds in MY 2025/26. In addition to the robust 2026 and 2027 renewable volume obligations, biomass-based diesel produced with canola oil from North America is now eligible for the 45Z producer tax credit. This credit incentivizes additional use of canola oil in biofuel compared to 2025 when it did not receive a credit. Canola oil use in food, feed, and other industrial use is also forecast to expand 4 percent from last year to 4.9 billion pounds. The canola oil price is forecast at 78 cents per pound, unchanged from last month’s forecast. The canola price is unchanged this month and forecast at 26.5 dollars per hundredweight. Sunflowerseed Outlook In MY 2026/27, U.S. sunflowerseed production is forecast to be marginally lower than the MY 2025/26 production on lower yield and higher area. In the latest Crop Production report, NASS released the first survey-based yield forecasts for sunflowerseed at 1,761 pounds per acre, down 5 percent from MY 2025/26. The farmers planted more sunflowerseed area in MY 2026/27 and are expected to harvest 1.3 million acres of sunflowerseed. The higher acreage is largely concentrated in North Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota. This increase was partially offset by lower area in Texas, Nebraska, and Kansas. Higher vegetable oil prices have supported sunflowerseed prices and farmer profitability, especially oil-type sunflowerseed which makes up more than 90 percent of total sunflowerseed acreage. -- 6 of 10 -- 7 Oil Crops Outlook: October 2026, OCS-26j, October 14, 2026 USDA, Economic Research Service The lower sunflowerseed production is more than offset by higher carry in stocks from MY 2025/26 and higher imports. As a result, U.S. sunflowerseed supply for MY 2026/27 is projected up 3 percent from MY 2025/26. With higher supplies, total demand for sunflowerseed is forecast to be up from last year, driven largely by domestic consumption. Sunflowerseed crush is forecast to remain elevated on increased demand for sunflowerseed oil. Sunflowerseed oil domestic use is forecast to grow 12 percent to 735 million pounds. Sunflowerseed oil is expected to fill part of the gap in food demand as a result of other domestic vegetable oils, like soybean oil, expected to be consumed in biofuel production. Non-oil use and residual is forecast higher than last year on the larger supply. The use is projected to be higher due to continued demand for birdseed. The yield is estimated at 3.21 metric tons per hectare, down nearly 5 percent from last month’s forecast due to dry weather in the major palm oil producing provinces. Since July, the dry weather persists in the southern Sumatra and Kalimantan provinces that account for approximately 60 percent of the total palm oil acreage in Indonesia. This continuous dryness is expected to have a negative impact on yield, as palm fruits require approximately 150−200 millimeters of water monthly and 2,400 millimeters per year. From June–September 2026, the cumulative precipitation reached more than 250 millimeters, compared with 800 millimeters during the same period last year. As a result of the lower palm oil production projection for MY 2026/27, Indonesia’s palm oil export forecast is reduced by 1.9 million metric tons this month to 21.6 million metric tons. The lower levels of palm oil exports from Indonesia are only partially offset by higher palm oil exports from Malaysia. In addition, world soybean oil and rapeseed oil exports are also raised, as some countries are expected to switch to these products in the face of tighter palm oil supplies.
